The requirement for vertical versus directional drilling ultimately depends on local geologic structure, bathymetry, and the hydraulic connection between the inland well and deep cold seawater. Site-specific investigations, including deep exploratory geophysical surveys and drilling, will be necessary to verify subsurface conditions and assess the feasibility of long-term GeoSWAC operation. For this preliminary analysis, however, economic metrics were estimated under the simplifying assumption that hydraulically connected, permeable formations containing 4°C–5°C water exist at a depth of roughly 1 km, regardless of the schematic isotherms in Figure 11. 4.2.1 Economic Metrics The conceptual GeoSWAC system consists of heat exchangers, circulating pumps, and surface piping connected to the campus distribution loop. Instead of chillers and cooling towers in the central chilled water plant, GeoSWAC relies on two inland wells: a deep production well (~1 km) to access cold water and a shallower injection well (~200 m) for discharge. This asymmetrical well configuration generally follows the well-established SWAC systems, where cold seawater is extracted from great depths and discharged at shallower levels to reduce infrastructure costs and environmental impact (Figure 1a). This approach also helps lower capital cost by reducing deep drilling requirements and simplifies subsurface engineering in this preliminary GeoSWAC design. Meanwhile, this configuration raises important questions, such as maintaining hydraulic balance, managing thermal dispersion, and evaluating potential thermal plume migration, especially in heterogeneous coastal aquifers. These subsurface dynamics need to be resolved through comprehensive future hydrogeologic modeling; this study presents a best- case conceptual scenario. In this scenario, it was assumed that 4°C cold water is continuously available at a depth of approximately 1 km, based on a simplified hydraulic equilibrium model in which the inland production well is statically connected to seawater at or near sea level. This connection implies that cold water at depth is under sufficient hydrostatic pressure to rise within the well column (the production well), enabling pumping from a shallower depth, assumed in this study as 100 m, instead of lifting cold water from the full 1 km. This assumption significantly reduces energy demand for pumping and associated operational costs. In addition, the water is assumed to have sufficiently low total dissolved solids that no additional filtering or pre-treatment is required before circulation through the heat exchangers (i.e., no water conditioning cost). This assumption is intended for first-order techno-economic evaluation and does not represent a site-specific water chemistry determination. Groundwater total dissolved solids, salinity, and fouling potential may vary spatially and would need to be characterized in detail for site-specific feasibility and system design.
